title: The Last Landfall
premise: Wendell Underhill, a disgraced railroad engineer drifting along abandoned rail lines with a stolen map of closed routes, has spent three years staying ahead of the debts and the law that ruined him. When he stumbles on a government survey team's vanished camp—gear intact, no tracks, no bodies—he realizes someone else is hiding in these hills, and that his own invisibility was always an illusion. Forced into an uneasy alliance with Mara Voss, the survey team's missing cartographer, Wendell must survive the monsoon in a leaking boat, evade the corrupt land syndicate that erased the surveyors, and decide whether justice is worth becoming visible again. The story ends at dry season's first light: Wendell surrenders himself to testify against the syndicate, trading his freedom for Mara's evidence and, for the first time, a place to belong.
about_author: Rafael Kavanagh is a former merchant marine who spent a decade working river freight routes across Southeast Asia before turning to writing full-time. His novels draw on firsthand knowledge of remote waterways, monsoon seasons, and the people who live deliberately off every map.

chapters.title: The Map of Closed Lines
chapters.summary: Wendell Underhill, POV. Riding a rusted handcar down an abandoned spur, Wendell explains his rule: never stop longer than two nights anywhere. A checkpoint ahead forces him onto an unmapped branch line. The beat is restless competence masking exhaustion—he is safe only because he never stays.

chapters.title: Two Nights in Kessel Junction
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. In a dying rail town, Wendell trades repair work for supplies and notices government survey markers freshly painted along the riverbank. An old stationmaster warns him that men in gray trucks have been asking about 'the engineer who knows the closed lines.' The beat: the past closing in.

chapters.title: Gear Without Ghosts
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Following the survey markers upriver, Wendell finds the survey camp abandoned mid-meal—kettle still warm, instruments wrapped, boats gone, no tracks leading out. He takes nothing but a waterlogged field notebook. The beat: dread; someone erased these people carefully.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Reeds
chapters.summary: Mara Voss, POV. Mara, the survey team's cartographer who survived by hiding underwater among the reeds, watches Wendell loot-then-not-loot the camp and decides he might be useful—or a threat. She follows him downstream. The beat: wary calculation from someone who trusts no one either.

chapters.title: Gray Trucks on the Old Causeway
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Syndicate enforcers sweep the valley looking for the notebook, burning the camp behind them. Wendell escapes along a collapsed viaduct but is spotted—and saved when Mara cuts their pursuers' tires. The beat: reluctant alliance forged under fire.

chapters.title: What the Notebook Says
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. In a flooded quarry cave, Mara reveals the truth: her team mapped water rights the Corvane Land Syndicate secretly bought, and Corvane erased them to bury the evidence. The notebook is the only copy. The beat: grief turning into purpose.

chapters.title: The Leaking Boat
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. With roads watched, they take a rotting skiff downriver toward the provincial archive where Mara can file the maps. The boat leaks; Wendell's engineering keeps it afloat through the first monsoon squall. The beat: grudging respect between two people used to being alone.

chapters.title: River People
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. They shelter with a floating fishing community led by Auntie Sef, who recognizes Wendell as the engineer whose testimony once helped river families win a dam dispute—before he disappeared. The beat: Wendell confronted with proof he once belonged somewhere.

chapters.title: The Price of Stopping
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Auntie Sef offers them shelter through the worst of the monsoon if Wendell repairs the community's failing pump barge. Staying means risk; leaving means drowning odds. He stays. The beat: choosing connection despite fear—the theme made personal.

chapters.title: Corvane Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. A syndicate lawyer finds them via a bribed fisherman and offers Wendell money and clean papers for the notebook, revealing Corvane framed him years ago to seize the rail lands he surveyed. The beat: rage and temptation; his ruin had authors.

chapters.title: Night Currents
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Wendell nearly takes the deal in a moment of despair, then discovers the lawyer's real plan: kill them both and sink the boat with the notebook aboard. He turns the trap around, barely. The beat: betrayal crystallizing resolve.

chapters.title: Monsoon Rising
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. The great storm hits early. The flotilla scatters; the pump barge breaks loose with children aboard. Wendell and Mara fight the flood to save them, and the repaired pump saves the barge. The beat: heroism witnessed—the town now claims him.

chapters.title: Afterwater
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Flood aftermath: drowned fields, a dead fisherman, Auntie Sef's quiet fury at Corvane's upstream levees built to divert flooding onto the river people. The stakes widen from survival to justice. The beat: mourning hardening into defiance.

chapters.title: The Archive at Harrow Bend
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. They reach the provincial archive town, but Corvane's men have sealed it, waiting. Mara proposes a mad route: the flooded rail tunnel Wendell's old map shows beneath the river bend. The beat: hope requiring trust in each other's skills.

chapters.title: Under the River
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. The tunnel passage: black water, collapsing brickwork, air pockets measured by Wendell's engineering instinct. They surface inside the archive district—but the notebook is soaked and its ink bleeding. The beat: triumph undercut by loss.

chapters.title: Ink and Memory
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. Mara can restore parts of the maps from memory, but a court will need corroboration—a witness with standing. Wendell realizes the witness must be him: the engineer Corvane framed, testifying would mean surrendering his freedom. The beat: the price of justice named aloud.

chapters.title: The Longest Two Nights
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Hiding in the archive's basement stacks while Corvane's men search floor by floor, Wendell drafts his testimony and finally tells Mara the whole story of his fall. The beat: confession; intimacy born of shared danger.

chapters.title: Dry Season's First Light
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. The rains break. Corvane's men corner them at the archive steps—but Auntie Sef arrives with thirty river boats and the fishing community standing witness, refusing to let the river's friends be taken quietly. The beat: belonging proven in action.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. In the provincial courthouse, Wendell testifies, surrendering himself as he speaks: the frame-up, the erased survey team, the levees. Mara's restored maps corroborate. Corvane's lawyer unravels. The beat: justice outside the law finally entering the law.

chapters.title: Sentencing
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. Wendell receives a reduced sentence—eighteen months—for obstruction long ago, his cooperation weighed heavily. Mara promises the river will be there when he gets out. The beat: bittersweet cost accepted without bitterness.

chapters.title: Lines Reopened
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Months into his sentence, Wendell is consulted on reopening the closed rail lines for flood recovery—his map, once his escape route, now a public good. Mara visits with news the survey team's families have filed suit against Corvane. The beat: redemption taking root.

chapters.title: Landfall
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Released at last, Wendell steps off a train at Kessel Junction, where Mara and Auntie Sef's boats wait on the high water. For the first time in years, he has somewhere to be and people expecting him. The beat: arrival—not at a place, but into a life.
